title: Problem Formulation & State Spaces
html:
Before an agent can search for a solution, the problem must be stated precisely: what a state is, which actions exist, what they do, what counts as the goal and what each step costs. A good formulation can shrink the search space by orders of magnitude.

The five components of a search problem

ComponentMeaningRoute finding (Romania)8-puzzle
Initial stateWhere the agent startsIn(Arad)A scrambled board
Actions(s)Moves applicable in state sDrive to a neighbouring citySlide the blank Up/Down/Left/Right
Transition model Result(s, a)The state an action leads toIn(Sibiu) after driving Arad → SibiuBoard with blank and tile swapped
Goal testIs s a goal?In(Bucharest)Tiles in order 0–8
Path costSum of step costs c(s, a, s′)Road kilometres1 per move

Initial state + actions + transition model define the state space — a graph whose nodes are states and edges are actions. A solution is an action sequence from the initial state to a goal; an optimal solution has the lowest path cost.

Formulating the 8-puzzle

Formulation decides the size of the space

ProblemFormulationStates
8-queensAdd queens anywhere, one at a time (64 squares, 8 queens)64 · 63 · … · 57 ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁴ sequences
8-queensOne queen per column, left to right, never attacking an earlier one2,057
8-puzzleAll boards9!/2 = 181,440 reachable
15-puzzleAll boards16!/2 ≈ 1.05 × 10¹³
Rubik's cubeAll positions≈ 4.3 × 10¹⁹
Key point

Abstraction is the art of formulation: drop every detail that doesn't affect the solution (the radio, the weather, the exact route between cities). A good abstraction is valid (every abstract solution maps to a real one) and useful (the abstract actions are easy to carry out).

Search trees, frontiers and repeated states

Search algorithms grow a search tree over the state space. Each node stores a state, its parent, the action that produced it, the path cost g and the depth. The frontier (open list) holds generated-but-not-expanded nodes; the order in which it is expanded is the only difference between most search strategies.

1
Initialise
Put a node for the initial state on the frontier.
2
Choose
Remove a node from the frontier according to the strategy (FIFO, LIFO, lowest cost…).
3
Test
If its state is a goal, return the path (follow parent links back).
4
Expand
Otherwise generate its children — one per applicable action — and add them to the frontier.
5
Repeat
Until the frontier is empty → failure.
Do

Use graph search: keep a reached/explored set so each state is expanded at most once — cycles and redundant paths (A→B→A→B…) are pruned.

Avoid

Plain tree search on a graph with cycles or many paths to the same state — it can loop forever or blow up exponentially.

Measuring a search strategy

CriterionQuestionSymbols used
CompletenessIs it guaranteed to find a solution when one exists?b = branching factor (max children per node)
Optimality (cost-optimal)Does it find the lowest-cost solution?d = depth of the shallowest goal
Time complexityHow many nodes does it generate?m = maximum depth of the state space (may be ∞)
Space complexityHow many nodes are in memory at once?C* = optimal cost, ε = smallest step cost
What are the components of a well-defined search problem?

Initial state, actions, transition model, goal test and path-cost function. The first three implicitly define the state space.

What is the difference between a state and a node?

A state is a configuration of the world. A node is a bookkeeping structure in the search tree: a state plus parent pointer, action, path cost and depth. The same state can appear in many nodes (reached by different paths).

Tree search vs graph search?

Graph search remembers visited states and never re-expands them, so it avoids loops and redundant paths at the cost of memory. Tree search keeps no such set and can revisit states indefinitely.
